pharm: Bacteriostatic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit
quick: 50 mg/kg/day IV in divided doses every 6 hours (up to 100 mg/kg/day severe)
Not applicable (IV); oral forms taken on empty stomach where available
Avoid near term - risk of grey baby syndrome in neonate
Excreted in breast milk; avoid breastfeeding during therapy
Caution; monitor levels - reduce in significant impairment
Reduce dose; impaired metabolism increases toxicity
CBC frequently; serum drug levels; neonatal levels
summary: Chloramphenicol is a potent broad-spectrum antibiotic reserved for serious infections where less toxic agents are ineffective or contraindicated. It carries a boxed warning for serious and fatal blood dyscrasias, including dose-independent aplastic anaemia. Use must be restricted and accompanied by close haematologic monitoring.
indications: Serious infections caused by susceptible organisms when less potentially dangerous agents are ineffective or contraindicated
Acute infections due to Salmonella typhi (typhoid fever)
Serious infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae, Rickettsia, lymphogranuloma-psittacosis group, and Gram-negative organisms causing bacteraemia/meningitis

dosage.d: 50 mg/kg/day IV in divided doses every 6 hours
dosage.n: Up to 100 mg/kg/day for severe infection (e.g. meningitis), then reduce
Up to 100 mg/kg/day in severe infection with caution
Lower doses and serum-level monitoring to avoid grey baby syndrome

admin: Administer by intravenous infusion of the sodium succinate form
It is desirable that patients be hospitalised for blood studies and observation
Obtain baseline and frequent (approx every 2 days) blood counts
Use the shortest effective course; do not use for trivial infections or prophylaxis
Monitor serum drug concentrations, especially in neonates, infants, and hepatic/renal impairment
moa: Chloramphenicol reversibly binds the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, inhibiting peptidyl transferase and thereby blocking peptide bond formation and bacterial protein synthesis. It is generally bacteriostatic.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity or toxic reaction to chloramphenicol
Use in trivial infections, prophylaxis, colds, flu or throat infections
monitor: Signs of grey baby syndrome in neonates

preg: Chloramphenicol crosses the placenta. Avoid during pregnancy, particularly at term and during labour, because of the risk of grey baby syndrome in the neonate. Use only if essential and no safer alternative exists.
lact: Chloramphenicol is excreted in human milk and may pose a risk of bone marrow toxicity to the infant; breastfeeding is not recommended during therapy.
renal: Reduce dose and monitor serum concentrations in significant renal impairment to avoid accumulation and toxicity.
hepatic: Chloramphenicol is metabolised in the liver; reduce the dose and monitor serum levels in hepatic impairment to avoid toxic accumulation.

major: Myelosuppressive agents - additive bone marrow toxicity
moderate: Iron, vitamin B12, folic acid - antagonised haematinic response
minor: May reduce efficacy of some bactericidal antibiotics (antagonism)
interactions.food: Not applicable for IV; minimal food relevance
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum chloramphenicol levels; frequent CBC essential

common: Reversible dose-related bone marrow suppression (anaemia, reticulocytopenia)
emergency: Grey baby syndrome (abdominal distension, cyanosis, cardiovascular collapse)

monitoring: Complete blood counts before and frequently during therapy (approx every 2 days)
Serum drug concentrations (peak/trough), especially neonates and organ impairment
Signs of grey baby syndrome in neonates
Reticulocyte count and signs of marrow toxicity
counsel: This is a potent antibiotic reserved for serious infection requiring close monitoring
Attend all blood tests as scheduled
Report unusual tiredness, bruising, bleeding, sore throat or fever immediately
Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine
pk: Active soon after IV administration as succinate is hydrolysed to free drug
Serum peak shortly after infusion; levels should be monitored
Approximately 1.5-4 hours in adults; prolonged in neonates and hepatic impairment
Reconstituted solution stored per label; protect from light
pearls: Boxed warning: serious and fatal blood dyscrasias, including idiosyncratic aplastic anaemia
Reserve for life-threatening infection with no safer alternative
Grey baby syndrome in neonates - avoid or monitor levels closely
Frequent CBC and serum-level monitoring are mandatory
Inhibits hepatic CYP - watch warfarin, phenytoin, sulfonylureas
missed: For scheduled inpatient IV therapy, a missed dose should be given as soon as recognised by the care team, maintaining the dosing interval; do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose increases the risk of bone marrow toxicity and, in neonates/infants, grey baby syndrome (vomiting, abdominal distension, cyanosis, hypotension, vasomotor collapse). Discontinue immediately; charcoal haemoperfusion or exchange transfusion may help; provide intensive supportive care.
